summary: The manuscript turns the deterministic-equivalent risk of ridge regression into a pilot-based forecaster of calibration learning curves (RPM) and evaluates it on 38 public NIR/MIR tasks. I checked Eqs. (1)-(5) against theory.py, ridge.py and forecasters.py. I reproduced the RPM point forecasts exactly from the code, verified the closed-form LOGO path against brute-force refits down to mu = 1e-12*lambda_1, and checked the risk formula and intercept factor by Monte Carlo with a real eigen-spectrum (within 3.5%). The core algebra is correct. The weaknesses are in how the theory is applied and validated. (1) The validity cut-off never binds for n0 <= 50, so up to 58% of the 53 path points are duplicates of the interpolation limit. The pre-registered 'unweighted' fit is therefore implicitly weighted by a grid artefact, and removing the duplicates shifts forecasts by 0.11 log-units on average. (2) The kappa-collapse, presented as a direct test of RPM's structural assumption, is compared with a non-equivalent reference and cannot distinguish effective sample sizes of n/2, n and 2n. (3) Ground-truth calibrations are strongly clustered (KSSL n = 6,400 contains about 2,355 profiles; ICRAF n = 1,600 contains 565 of 689 pool profiles) while the theory and pilots assume i.i.d. samples. (4) The theory's oracle-penalty risk is compared with LOGO-tuned ridge; the gap is 0.107 log-units at n = 50 and 0.011 at n = 1,600, about 14% of the typical slope. (5) The headline slope claims are confounded with the n-range of each curve: pool size correlates with the slope more strongly than the noise fraction, and slopes over n = 50-400 are about twice those over n >= 400. The identifiability argument, the alignment-exponent estimates and the role of unlabelled spectra are also stated more strongly than the evidence supports.
strengths: Eqs. (2)-(3) are implemented correctly. A Monte-Carlo check with the ICRAF-MIR pool eigen-spectrum (Gaussian design, n = 25-100) agreed with the theory within -0.2% to -3.5% in MSE, including the (1 + 1/n) intercept factor.

The closed-form weighted LOGO path (ridge.py) is exact: the hat-matrix construction with weighted centring is algebraically correct, and it matched SVD-based brute-force LOO to relative errors of 1e-9 to 5e-6 even at mu = 1e-12*lambda_1 on real SNV spectra.
The code is fully reproducible: re-running fit_rpm/forecast_theory with the documented seeds reproduces the stored RPM forecasts to 1e-15.
The design is transparent: pre-registration, time-stamped decision log, negative results (RPM-T, the decision metric) reported, and simple competitors (FLAT, SLOPE-T) included on identical pilots.

issues.title: The df2/n0 <= 0.8 validity cut-off never applies at n0 <= 50, so the pre-registered fit (Eq. 5, w_j = 1) is dominated by duplicate near-interpolation points, and RPM's accuracy depends on the arbitrary lower end of the penalty grid
issues.description: Section 2.3 says Eq. (5) is fitted 'over the path points with df2/n0 <= 0.8'. The implied purpose is to drop the weakly regularised path points where LOGO errors are heavy-tailed. For n0 = 25 and 50 the cut-off never binds: at kappa_min(n0), df2/n_eff is only 0.69-0.79 in every task. All 53 grid points therefore enter the fit. Because the grid is log-uniform in mu down to 1e-12*lambda_1 and kappa saturates at kappa_min when n0 < rank, between 7 and 31 of the 53 points (task-dependent) sit within 5% of kappa_min. They are near-identical copies of the same ridgeless LOGO error. The 'unweighted' pre-registered fit is thus an implicitly weighted fit that gives up to ~58% of the weight to the single most variable point of the path. The weight is set by how far the grid extends below kappa_min, a choice with no statistical justification. This is very likely the root cause of the 'pull towards optimistic values' that motivated RPM-w (EXPERIMENT_LOG 19:24-19:27). RPM-w's inverse-variance weights also count each duplicate separately. The 0.5/0.95 cut-off ablation (Table 3) cannot detect the problem, because 0.95 changes nothing at n0 <= 50.
issues.evidence: Recomputed with theory.solve_kappa/df2_of on the pool eigen-spectra stored in results/raw/truth_*.npz (script /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R2/kappa_grid.py). At n0 = 25 the number of points within 5% of kappa_min is 13 (Tecator) to 31 (KSSL-MIR); max df2/n_eff is 0.69-0.79, so all 53 points are retained. At n0 = 50 it is 7-26 for most tasks. Re-fit with the code's own fit_rpm on the exact pilots (seeds as in forecast_experiment.py; my RPM point forecasts reproduce raw_results.csv to 1e-15). Removing only the kappa-duplicates (keeping one point per 5% kappa step) changed the n0 <= 50 forecasts by a mean of 0.113 log-units (max 0.452). Pooled bias moved from +0.040 to +0.101 and pooled error from 0.261 to 0.277 (Mango:DM n0 = 25: 0.181 -> 0.272; ICRAF-MIR:OC n0 = 25: 0.345 -> 0.271) over 7 tasks (Mango, Tecator:fat, Diesel:bp50, Tablets, ICRAF-MIR:OC, Neospectra-NIR:pH, KSSL-VisNIR:clay; script /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R2/dedup.py). These shifts are larger than the RPM-FLAT (0.021) and RPM-SLOPE-T (0.023) differences in Table 2.
issues.corrective_action: Define the path on kappa rather than mu: use a grid uniform in log kappa(n_eff, mu), or weight path points by their spacing in log kappa (quadrature weights) so that the fit approximates an integral over the observed kappa range. Alternatively, make the cut-off one that actually removes the interpolation regime, for example kappa >= c*kappa_min. Report sensitivity of RPM and RPM-w to the lower grid limit (1e-12, 1e-8, 1e-6) and to the cut-off at n0 = 25/50. Explain in Section 2.3 why the 'unweighted' fit is in fact weighted, and revisit the explanation for RPM-w.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run RPM and RPM-w (point forecasts plus bootstrap) on all 2,640 existing pilots with (a) a kappa-uniform path and (b) mu-grid lower limits of 1e-8 and 1e-6. Report Table 2 and the bias for each. About 1 CPU-hour; no new data needed.

issues.title: The kappa-collapse test (Fig. 2b, Table S3) uses a non-comparable reference and cannot distinguish the theory's n-to-kappa mapping from mappings wrong by a factor of two in n
issues.description: Section 4.1 presents the collapse as a direct test of the structural assumption of RPM: n and mu act only through kappa(n, mu) plus the prefactor. The evidence is 0.041 (collapse) versus 0.519 (raw penalty). The two numbers are not computed on the same data. In experiments/analysis.py:collapse_dispersion, the collapse statistic is restricted to path points with df2/n < 0.8 and to the overlap of the kappa ranges. The reference instead uses all 53 penalties without the prefactor, including the near-interpolation region where small-n errors explode. The reference therefore measures mostly the interpolation peak. More importantly, the statistic has little power against the alternative that matters for forecasting, namely an error in the effective sample size. A factor of two in effective n equals one doubling of n, which is the 8% RMSE effect the paper forecasts.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from results/raw/truth_*.npz (scripts /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R2/collapse.py, collapse2.py, collapse3.py), 31 tasks. (i) Same kappa window as the paper, no kappa mapping, errors at fixed mu with the prefactor only: median SD 0.080, not 0.519. (ii) Raw log test MSE at fixed mu in the same window: 0.108. (iii) On a window common to all mappings, the median across-n SD is 0.0062, 0.0059 and 0.0069 when kappa is computed with n/2, n and 2n; only n/8 is clearly worse (0.029), while log N varies by about 0.85 over the window. (iv) In the paper's own window, kappa computed with n/4 gives a smaller dispersion (0.021) than the theory's mapping (0.041), because the statistic depends on the window.
issues.corrective_action: Report the collapse against fair nulls on identical points (same window, same mu set, with and without the prefactor). Profile the dispersion over an effective-sample-size scaling c (kappa computed at c*n) and report the c that minimises dispersion, with a CI from the repetitions. State explicitly the precision with which the collapse validates the mapping (here no better than a factor of about two in n). Rephrase Section 4.1 and the Fig. 2 caption: the collapse supports a kappa-type reparametrisation, not the exact n-dependence that RPM extrapolates.

issues.title: Ground-truth calibrations are clustered (many soil layers per profile), whereas Eq. (2) and the pilots treat n as independent samples. The effective n of large calibrations is much smaller than n
issues.description: Eq. (2) is derived for n i.i.d. samples. Pilots (25-200 samples drawn at random from the pool) are almost i.i.d. at the group level. The ground-truth calibrations at large n are not. learning_curves.truth_curve draws individual samples (rng.choice(pool, n)), so a calibration of thousands of layers contains far fewer profiles, and the test set is group-disjoint. With strong within-profile correlation of y (and of the spectra), the effective number of independent units grows much more slowly than n at large n. Consequences: (a) the large-n flattening of the soil curves, and hence the '8.3% per doubling' and the 'noise floor sets the slope' narrative, partly reflect running out of distinct profiles; (b) the theory-validity check (Section 4.1) and RPM's extrapolation use n, not the number of independent units; (c) n_pool correlates with the slope (see R2-C01-05). Section 3.2 discusses groups only as leakage control, not as a violation of the theory's i.i.d. premise.
issues.evidence: Loaded the tasks with the authors' loader (script /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R2/groups.py). KSSL-MIR:OC pool: 12,002 layers in 2,580 groups (mean 4.65 per group); an n = 6,400 calibration contains about 2,355 distinct groups. ICRAF-MIR:OC pool: 2,774 layers in 689 groups; n = 1,600 contains about 565 groups (82% of all pool groups) and n = 200 contains 164. Within-group intraclass correlation of y (rough one-way ANOVA): 0.57 (KSSL-MIR OC), 0.49 (ICRAF-MIR OC), 0.82 (AfSIS1-MIR OC), 0.38 (Neospectra OC). Pilots of 25 contain 24.4-25.0 distinct groups.
issues.corrective_action: Define n consistently as the number of independent units. Either draw ground-truth calibrations by whole groups (and index the curve by the number of groups, or by layers with a stated sampling design), or keep one layer per profile for the theory analyses. Report how slopes, theory-validity errors and forecast errors change. Add a design-effect discussion to Sections 2.1 and 5.
issues.proposed_experiment: Recompute the ground-truth learning curves for the 23 soil tasks with group-wise sampling (n = number of profiles, or a fixed one-layer-per-profile subsample). Repeat the slope analysis, the theory-validity fit and the pilot evaluation against these curves.

issues.title: Estimand mismatch: the theory forecasts the oracle-penalty risk min_mu E(n, mu), but the ground truth is LOGO-tuned ridge. The gap depends strongly on n and is not modelled
issues.description: Section 2.2 states that a CV-tuned calibration 'is approximated by the minimum over the penalty grid', without quantifying the approximation. The expected excess error of CV tuning over the oracle penalty is largest at small n and vanishes at large n. Ignoring it (a) inflates the theory-validity error (Section 4.1), (b) makes the true curves steeper than any oracle-risk curve, so part of the empirical slope comes from less tuning noise, not from learning new modes, and (c) biases RPM's forecasts optimistically by an amount that depends on the horizon.
issues.evidence: From results/raw/truth_*.npz, the gap 0.5*log(ridge_mse / min_mu ridge_mu_mse) (tuned ridge vs best fixed penalty of the same averaged curve) has mean (median) 0.107 (0.075) at n = 50, 0.074 (0.042) at 100, 0.066 (0.030) at 200, 0.034 (0.019) at 400 and 0.011 (0.008) at 1600. Maxima: 0.94 (Diesel:total, n = 200), 0.30 (Tecator:fat, n = 50), 0.27 (KSSL-VisNIR:pH, n = 50). Median slope per doubling is -0.086 for the tuned curves and -0.075 for the oracle curves, so about 14% of the median slope is due to the tuning gap. The theory-validity table T9 compares oracle theory with tuned truth.
issues.corrective_action: Either (i) add a model of the selection cost to the forecast (for example, simulate LOGO selection inside the theory, or add an approximate selection-variance term), or (ii) report all accuracy and validity metrics also against the oracle curve min_mu ridge_mu_mse, which is already stored. Discuss the size of the gap in Sections 2.2 and 4.1, and in the slope analysis (Section 4.2).

issues.title: Two slope claims are confounded with the n-range over which each slope is fitted: 'remarkably similar' slopes (8.3% per doubling) and 'noise fraction is the dominant term'. SLOPE-T transfers slopes across different ranges
issues.description: Slopes are fitted by one straight line of log RMSE against log2 n over each task's whole ground-truth curve (analysis.add_slope_transfer). The ranges differ: 50-100 for Tecator/CGL, 50-6,400 for KSSL. The curves are strongly concave in log-log coordinates, so the fitted slope depends mechanically on the range. Pool size, which sets the range, is a stronger single correlate of the slope than the noise fraction. The noise fraction keeps only a moderate partial association once pool size is controlled. The abstract's 'slopes were governed mainly by the irreducible-noise fraction' is therefore not supported. SLOPE-T applies a median slope fitted mostly over 50-1,600/6,400 soil curves to other tasks' horizons of 2n0 to n_max.
issues.evidence: tables/T17_posthoc_slope_explanation.md shows Spearman rho(slope, n_pool) = 0.624 (p = 2.8e-5), larger than rho(slope, noise_frac) = 0.590. Recomputed from results/alignment_exponents.csv and slope_per_doubling.csv: partial rank correlation of slope with noise fraction given n_pool = 0.38, and with n_pool given noise fraction = 0.45; rho(noise_frac, n_pool) = 0.55. Concavity in the 17 tasks with curves to >= 1,600: median slope -0.101 per doubling over n = 50-400 versus -0.048 over n >= 400.
issues.corrective_action: Compute slopes over a common n-range, or a range defined relative to n0 (for example, the slope between n and 4n at fixed n), or report a model-based slope at fixed n. Redo the slope regression with the n-range (or n_pool) as a covariate. Make SLOPE-T ratio- and range-specific. Rephrase the abstract, Section 4.2 and the conclusions accordingly.

issues.title: The identifiability statement (Section 2.4) is asserted as absolute without proof, and the RPM-T 'noise-floor collapse' partly reflects an unregularised sigma^2 parametrisation
issues.description: Section 2.4 says that 'no pilot, however analysed, can separate target power hidden in weak modes from irreducible noise'. What follows from Eq. (3) is narrower. On kappa >= kappa_min(n0), modes with lambda_k << kappa_min contribute s_k(1 - O(lambda_k/kappa)) to N(kappa), so the path confounds sigma^2 with tail power only approximately. Other statistics of the pilot, such as the marginal likelihood (which the authors use in the ML-II ablation) or replicate measurements, carry some information. The non-identifiability is therefore an asymptotic, weak-identification property, not a theorem. The catastrophic RPM-T failures (mean signed log error -6.71) also arise because fit_rpm lets log sigma^2 go to log(max e) - 25. That is about 1e-11 of the largest path error, effectively zero, with no prior. A model with a mild lower bound or a prior on the noise fraction would fail far less badly. The failure magnitude says as much about the parametrisation as about identifiability.
issues.evidence: forecasters.py fit_rpm: lower bound ls_lo = np.log(v) - 25 for log sigma^2 (line 106 of the current file; lines 107-109 in the version that produced the results). The working-tree code now has an optional sigma2_floor argument and a dicker_noise estimator (uncommitted changes labelled 'review cycle 1'). Its default (None) leaves the old bound unchanged, and the reported results and manuscript do not use it. Manuscript Section 4.4: noise fraction for KSSL-MIR OC '< 10^-4' versus 0.018 in the large-sample fit; collapse in 21% of RPM-T pilots at n0 = 25. EXPERIMENT_LOG 16:05 mentions a 'noise-floor guard' hypothesis that was not tested.
issues.corrective_action: State the identifiability result formally: the confounding of sigma^2 with sum_{lambda_k << kappa_min} s_k in N(kappa), with its error terms. Soften 'however analysed' to 'from the regularisation path'. Add a sensitivity analysis in which RPM-T has a weak prior or lower bound on sigma^2/var(y), for example the 5th percentile of the large-sample noise fractions of the other sources. This shows whether the failure is intrinsic or a consequence of the parametrisation.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run RPM-T on the existing pilots with a leave-one-source-out lower bound or log-normal prior on the noise fraction. Report the error, the bias and the share of collapsed fits. Takes minutes; no new data.

issues.title: Alignment exponents r are point estimates from a single three-parameter path fit, reported without uncertainty. Small-pool estimates use a distorted sample eigen-spectrum, and the physical interpretation by region is not supported
issues.description: Section 4.2 says r < 1 'in all 38 tasks' and explains the Vis/NIR vs MIR difference physically (median 0.36 vs 0.62). Four problems. (i) r is estimated jointly with tau^2 and sigma^2 from one LOGO path per task, and r and sigma^2 trade off. No confidence interval or profile is reported. (ii) For Diesel (N_pool/p = 1.43-1.48) and CGL (1.49), the 'population' eigen-spectrum is a sample spectrum from fewer than 1.5 samples per variable. Small eigenvalues are then strongly biased (Marchenko-Pastur spreading), which distorts both the kappa mapping and r. These are also the tasks with the largest theory-validity errors (Diesel:total 0.38, CGL:lactate 0.33, CGL:moisture 0.29), which the paper attributes only to non-random sampling. (iii) The Vis/NIR/SWNIR group consists of only three spectral libraries (four analytes of ICRAF-VisNIR and of KSSL-VisNIR share the same eigen-spectrum, plus Mango), so the effective sample is n = 3. (iv) The region difference is partly an eigen-decay effect, which undermines both the chemical interpretation and the transfer of a single r across instruments in RPM-T.
issues.evidence: results/alignment_exponents.csv: n_pool = 286-296 for Diesel (p = 200) and 173 for CGL (p = 116). Recomputed eigen-decay exponents alpha (log lambda_k vs log k, k <= 60): Vis/NIR/SWNIR 3.83, MIR soil 2.80. The implied decay of target power per mode index, alpha*r, is 1.38 vs 1.74, a much smaller relative difference than r itself (0.36 vs 0.62). r_loso_prior spans only 0.523-0.575, even though region medians differ by 0.26.
issues.corrective_action: Give group-bootstrap (or profile-likelihood) CIs for r and sigma^2/var(y) for every task. Show the sensitivity of r to eigenvalue shrinkage (for example, nonlinear shrinkage) for pools with N/p < 3. Treat analytes sharing a library as clustered when comparing regions. Present the region interpretation as a hypothesis. Discuss whether r is a transferable quantity across eigen-decays (consider transferring alpha*r instead).
issues.proposed_experiment: Group bootstrap (for example, 50 replicates) of the full-pool path fit for each task to obtain CIs for r and the noise fraction. Repeat for Diesel/CGL/Tecator with a shrinkage-corrected eigen-spectrum.

issues.title: The paper's own ablations contradict the role it gives to unlabelled spectra
issues.description: The Introduction, Section 2.3 (observation 1) and Section 2.4 present the eigen-spectrum from cheap unlabelled spectra as a key measured ingredient: 'this is measured, not assumed'. The pre-registered ablation shows that it adds nothing under r = 1. Under the transferred exponent it is harmful: the pilot-only spectrum (rank n0 - 1, no weak-mode tail) is much more accurate than the pool spectrum, presumably because the truncated spectrum removes the tail-power/noise ambiguity. The manuscript's conclusion that 'unlabelled spectra are therefore not what limits these forecasts' understates this. In practice, the method's extrapolation skill does not come from the measured tail.
issues.evidence: Table 3: pilot-only covariance 0.254 vs RPM 0.242 (Holm p = 1.000); 250 unlabelled spectra 0.239. Section 4.6: RPM-T 0.392 vs RPM-T-pilotcov 0.258 (Holm p = 0.0007); RPM-T-pilotcov+tail 0.469.
issues.corrective_action: Revise the Introduction, Section 2.3 and Section 2.4 so that they say what the ablations show: with r fixed the measured spectral tail is immaterial, and with r < 1 it is harmful. Discuss why truncation helps, since it amounts to an implicit noise-floor assumption. Remove or qualify 'measured, not assumed' as an advantage of RPM.

issues.title: Several equations differ from the code: n0 vs n_eff in Eq. (4)/(5), the cut-off denominator, an undocumented cut-off fallback, the per-sample penalty in LOGO refits, and an unvalidated intercept factor
issues.description: (a) Eq. (4) and the cut-off use n0. The code uses n_eff = n0 - mean group size of the pilot (forecasters.py RPMForecaster.fit_forecast, lines 156-157 of the current file), and the cut-off is applied to df2/n_eff (_path_points, line 61). For variable group sizes, the size-biased mean training size of the LOGO fits is n0 - sum(s_g^2)/n0, not n0 - mean(s_g). (b) If fewer than 3 points pass, the cut-off is silently relaxed to 0.95 (fit_rpm, lines 79-84); this is not documented. (c) The closed-form LOGO refits keep the absolute penalty n0*mu on n0 - s_g samples, so their per-sample penalty is mu*n0/(n0 - s_g), whereas kappa is solved with mu at n_eff. (d) The (1 + 1/n) intercept factor of Eq. (3) is stated without derivation or citation. The unit test (test_core_math.py line 85, tolerance 6% at n >= 40) cannot detect a factor of 2.5%. My Monte-Carlo check with the ICRAF-MIR spectrum and Gaussian design gave theory/MC - 1 between -0.2% and -3.5% for n = 25-100, so the approximation is adequate. It should nevertheless be documented and validated at n0 = 25.
issues.evidence: Code lines cited above. Monte-Carlo script /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R2/mc_intercept.py (400 replicates per cell, 20,000 test samples).
issues.corrective_action: Write Eqs. (4)-(5) exactly as implemented (n_eff, per-sample penalty, fallback rule). Give a reference or short derivation for the intercept factor. Extend the unit test to n0 = 25 with a tolerance below 2%.

issues.title: The Bayesian bootstrap and the RPM-w weights ignore the group structure and the correlation between path points, so the bands reflect pilot sampling noise only
issues.description: Dirichlet weights are drawn per sample (forecasters.py RPMForecaster.fit_forecast, line 169 of the current file), although the LOGO path is grouped and pilots of 200 soil samples contain repeated groups. The eigen-spectrum and r are held fixed, so the bands cannot reflect uncertainty in the parts of the model that drive the extrapolation. The delta-method variance used for RPM-w (ridge.py ridge_cv_path, lines 71-74) treats squared residuals as independent across samples within a group, and treats the 53 nearly perfectly correlated, partly duplicated path points as independent observations. The weights are also estimated from the same residuals they weight. The under-coverage reported in Section 4.5 (42.3%/58.3%) therefore follows largely from how the bands are constructed.
issues.evidence: ICRAF-MIR:OC pilots of 200 contain about 164 distinct groups (script /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R2/groups.py). The bootstrap band centre is offset from the point forecast by +0.052 log-units at n0 = 25 and -0.024 at n0 = 200 (raw_results.csv, (lo80 + hi80)/2 vs fc_logrmse).
issues.corrective_action: Use group-level (cluster) Dirichlet weights, and resample the unlabelled spectra for the eigen-spectrum. State clearly in Sections 2.3 and 4.5 that the bands are conditional on r = 1 and on the fixed eigen-spectrum. Describe the RPM-w weights as heuristic rather than inverse-variance (GLS) weights.

issues.title: The DF-OLS baseline is misspecified for ridge, so its significant inferiority is not informative
issues.description: dfols_forecast uses s^2 = RSS/(n0 - df - 1) with df = tr(H) of ridge. For a linear smoother the residual degrees of freedom are n0 - 2tr(H) + tr(H'H). The denominator is also clipped at 1, and with p > n0 at small penalties the training RSS is near zero. The forecast s^2(1 + 1/n + df/(n - df - 1)) then converges to an optimistic s^2. The method is described as 'a classical fixed-complexity formula', but it is not an established chemometric procedure.
issues.evidence: forecasters.py dfols_forecast (lines 312-323 of the current file). Table 2: DF-OLS bias -1.161, mean error 1.272.
issues.corrective_action: Either implement the formula with the correct residual degrees of freedom and a penalty rescaled with n, or present DF-OLS as an illustrative strawman and drop it from the inferential claims (Holm family).

issues.title: The simulation (E0) gives RPM the true population eigen-spectrum and has an atypical eigen-decay; it also has a self-contradictory statement and wrong cross-references
issues.description: simulation.py passes the true lambda to RPMForecaster (line 61), so E0 does not test eigen-spectrum estimation. It uses a single beta draw per scenario and lambda_k = k^-1.6, whereas the real SNV spectra decay much faster (alpha 2.8-3.9 over k <= 60, and lambda spans about 9 orders of magnitude over 212 modes). The statement 'When the assumptions hold, the small pilot, not the theory, limits accuracy' is therefore conditional on oracle knowledge of lambda. Section 4.7 says 'RPM was the most accurate forecaster (0.138; RPM-w 0.137)', which contradicts the numbers it gives. It also cites the simulation as Supplementary Tables S21-S22, which are the decision and gain tables; the simulation is S26-S27.
issues.evidence: experiments/simulation.py lines 24-33 (_make) and 61. manuscript_full.md line 241. supplementary_full.md: Table S21 (decision metric), S22 (gain), S26/S27 (simulation).
issues.corrective_action: Add a simulation arm in which the eigen-spectrum is estimated from a finite unlabelled set, using an eigen-decay matched to the real spectra and several beta draws. Correct the wording and the cross-references.
issues.proposed_experiment: E0 rerun with lambda estimated from 250 and 2,000 unlabelled Gaussian spectra, eigen-decay alpha = 3, and 10 beta draws per scenario. Takes minutes.

note_on_versions: The review covers the manuscript, results and tables as submitted, which were generated by the committed code. During the review, uncommitted edits appeared in code/src/models/forecasters.py (sigma2_floor option, log-scale delta-method bands for the curve baselines, nested CV, Dicker noise estimator, Wei et al. exponent) and code/src/training/learning_curves.py (n = 25 added to TRUTH_GRID, per-repetition MSE stored). None of these changes is reflected in the reported numbers. Line numbers refer to the current working-tree files unless stated otherwise.
recommendation_rationale: No issue invalidates the central negative findings (power-law extrapolation is optimistic, and the pilot's CV error with a typical slope is as good as any method). However, several methodological claims that carry the paper's theoretical contribution are not supported at the precision claimed. The kappa-collapse validation lacks discriminating power. The fitted path is dominated by a grid artefact that affects the pre-registered method's bias. The i.i.d. theory is tested against clustered ground-truth calibrations. The oracle-vs-tuned estimand gap is unmodelled. The slope/noise-fraction conclusion is confounded with the n-range. These problems can be fixed with re-analysis and modest re-runs on existing data (kappa-uniform path, group-wise truth curves, fair collapse nulls, range-matched slopes), but the conclusions in Sections 4.1-4.2 and the abstract must be revised accordingly.
